root.note: Past participle of obligare ‘to bind’. A semi-learned word: it kept more of its Latin shape than inherited words.

history: When you say obrigado, you are saying ‘I am obliged to you’. The word is Latin obligatus, ‘bound’, with the l turned into r, as in igreja and branco. Because it describes the speaker, it agrees with the speaker: a man says obrigado, a woman says obrigada, whoever they are thanking. Many learners get this wrong at first. Then there is the famous story that Japanese arigatō comes from obrigado, brought by Portuguese sailors. It is a good story, and it is wrong. Arigatō comes from the Japanese adjective arigatai, ‘rare, hard to have’, and that word was in use before any Portuguese ship reached Japan. The likeness is pure coincidence.
historyEinfach: Obrigado means ‘thank you’. Word for word, it means ‘I am obliged’. It comes from Latin obligatus. A man says obrigado, a woman says obrigada. Many people think that Japanese arigatō comes from obrigado. That is not true: arigatō is an old Japanese word.

chain: Classical Japanese arigatashi ‘rare, hard to have’
elsewhere.text: It sounds like obrigado, but it is a native Japanese word, older than the first Portuguese visit.
Old-fashioned English ‘much obliged’ is exactly the Portuguese idea of thanks.
